passages.nngroupWhich: Christian Rohrer, NN/g, 17 Jul 2022 (reviewed 15 Jul 2026): 20 methods mapped on a 3-dimensional framework: attitudinal vs behavioral (what people say vs what they do), qualitative vs quantitative (why / how to fix vs how many / how much; collected directly vs through an instrument), and context of product use (natural, scripted, limited, not using the product). Time dimension: Strategize (generative: field studies, diary studies, interviews, surveys, participatory design, concept testing), Design (formative: card sorting, tree testing, usability testing, remote moderated and unmoderated testing), Launch and Assess (summative: usability benchmarking, unmoderated UX testing, A/B testing, clickstream analytics, surveys). Nearly every project benefits from combining methods; many teams rely on one or two familiar ones.

paaNote: Sources: Ahrefs serp-overview 'question' rows 2026-10-24 for the primary and its 6 same-intent variants (lesson 2026-10-23). Mapping (first sentence = direct answer): the 4 generic academic questions ('7 types of research methods', '7 basic research methods', '7 major types of research', 'four types of research methods', '7 types of qualitative research methods') -> ONE disambiguation H3 inside H2 1 'How do UX research methods relate to academic research types?': no single standard list of 7 exists; academic texts group quantitative designs (commonly descriptive, correlational, quasi-experimental, experimental) and qualitative approaches (Creswell and Poth name 5: narrative, phenomenology, grounded theory, ethnography, case study); then the UX meaning: UX research methods are applied techniques chosen by product question, and the ethnography idea survives as field studies and contextual inquiry. Fact-checker confirms both lists before print; if the 4 quantitative designs cannot be sourced, print only the Creswell list and say textbooks differ. 'Is UX research being replaced by AI?' -> FAQ 1 (No; NN/g synthetic users). 'Different types of user research methods' -> H2 3. '5-user rule' -> FAQ 2. 'Is user research the same as UX research' + 'difference between user research and UX research' -> H3 in H2 1 (Yes, same thing; hub says 'UX research, also called user research'). 'Three types of user testing' -> FAQ 3 (sources disagree; answer with moderated vs unmoderated, qualitative vs quantitative, remote vs in-person, hub usability wording). 'Five steps of UX research' -> FAQ 4 (our 5 hub steps, deep link to hub process section; no process H2, the hub owns it). 'What is the UX methodology' -> H3 'Method, methodology or technique?' in H2 1. 'Most effective research techniques' -> first sentence of H2 2 (the effective one is the one that answers your question; no universal best). Dropped with reasons: 'What are the 7 pillars of UX design?' (methodology variant SERP; a UX design facets question, Morville's honeycomb, not research methods), 'What are the different types of UX?' (design disciplines, off-intent), 'Is UX research still in demand?' (career/job-market question; no verifiable US labor statistic for UX researchers exists in BLS; off-intent for a buyer guide). QA must not fail the page for these three.

siteFacts.definition: Hub: 'UX research, also called user research, is the systematic study of user goals, behaviours and problems through interviews, observation and testing, conducted to guide product and design decisions.' 2 modes: generative finds what to build, evaluative checks whether a design works.
siteFacts.deliverables: Hub 6 deliverables: research plan; user interviews (10-15 one-hour interviews); contextual inquiry (observe 4-6 users in the real work setting); card sort and tree test (Optimal Workshop, 30-50 participants); personas (2-4) and journey maps (1 per persona); Jobs to be Done opportunity map.
siteFacts.process: Hub 5 steps, 4-8 weeks (20-40 working days): research framing (2-4 days), participant recruitment (3-6 days), generative fieldwork (7-15 days: user interviews and contextual inquiry), evaluative studies (4-8 days: card sorts, tree tests and concept tests), synthesis and readout (4-7 days: tagged in Dovetail, personas, journey maps, JTBD opportunity map, 90-minute readout). Quote these step bodies when the post ties a method to a step (lesson 2026-10-20); never assign an output to a step whose body does not name it.
siteFacts.price: $25,000-$60,000 for the programme; depends on user groups, participants, number of methods, recruitment difficulty (hub cost H2). State once with the deep link; no cost section.
siteFacts.participants: Hub FAQ: 10-15 interview participants per user group; 5 per round of qualitative usability testing (NN/g). Usability hub FAQ: 5 users per qualitative round, 40 for a quantitative test (NN/g). Usability hub: moderated has a researcher present; unmoderated runs on tools such as Maze without a researcher; A/B testing needs enough traffic to reach statistical significance; a single usability round takes 1-3 weeks.
siteFacts.remote: Hub FAQ: remote UX research runs user interviews and card sorts over video calls and online tools (Zoom, Optimal Workshop); contextual inquiry needs on-site visits (CONFLICT 1 of the contextual-inquiry brief still open; in this post say 'in our programme, contextual inquiry runs on-site').
siteFacts.ai: home.ts: 'We use AI to accelerate production. The judgment about what to design comes from research and pattern recognition across 200+ products.' Usable for FAQ 1 as our stance.

serpGaps: Question first: every ranking page is organised by method (a list of 11-20 methods) or by stage; only formbricks maps questions to methods, in one table without reasoning or sources. None starts from the product decision a team faces and routes it to a method with the reason.

Method vs methodology vs technique: NN/g, Maze, Figma and User Interviews use the words interchangeably; User Interviews' own module is titled 'Methodologies' and Figma calls activities 'methodologies'. Nobody defines the three levels with one example chain.

Sourced numbers: Maze, Figma, progress, Leanlab and Contentsquare give no sample sizes or study lengths; formbricks gives ranges with no source. We give NN/g 5 qual / 40 quant, NN/g focus group size, and the hub's own 10-15 interviews, 4-6 contextual inquiry users and 30-50 card-sort participants, each with the source.

Combination recipe: NN/g says to combine; figr gives one interview-then-survey example. Nobody shows a full sequence (analytics finds where -> interviews find why -> card sort/tree test fixes structure -> usability test checks the fix -> A/B test measures it) with what each step hands the next.
Constraints: Maze mentions 'buy-in, budget and time' in one line; nobody says which methods survive a small budget and what you lose with each shortcut.

Mistakes: no ranking page lists the common method-choice errors (asking users to predict future behavior, surveys for why questions, 5 users for a metric, testing IA in interviews, one method for everything).
AI: PAA asks whether UX research is being replaced by AI; no ranking methods page answers it. NN/g's synthetic-users article (Rosala and Moran 2024) gives a sourced answer.
Stage map tied to a real programme: stage lists exist (NN/g, Figma) but none shows how a real engagement sequences them in days.

outline.answerHint: UX research methods are the techniques a product team uses to collect evidence about users, for example user interviews, surveys, card sorting and usability testing, and each one answers a different kind of research question. Teams also call them user research methods or UX research techniques.
points: Intro before this H2 (three-question triage, see variety): 3 illustrative questions from one product meeting, each needing a different method; keyword in the first sentence or within 60 words (carrier above). Then one sentence on what the guide gives: a question router, the NN/g dimensions, a stage map, a method table with sample sizes, a combination recipe and the mistakes to avoid.
UP link within the first 300 words, anchor exactly 'UX research services' (required by the orchestrator), e.g. 'our UX research services combine five of these methods in one programme'.
Definition paragraph: parent = UX research (hub definition: 'also called user research'); expand 'user experience (UX)' once; UX research serves user-centered design (ISO 9241-210, hub wording).

H3 'Method, methodology or technique?' (PAA 'What is the UX methodology?'; owner's concept binding): a methodology is the strategy and reasoning behind the study (e.g. user-centered design, or an ethnographic approach); a method is the procedure that collects data (e.g. usability testing); a technique is a specific way of running part of a method (e.g. the think-aloud protocol inside a usability test, or a five-second test). Source the method/methodology split to Dovetail (7 Mar 2023) or describe it as common usage; 'technique' level is our framing, say so plainly. One sentence: in everyday UX writing the three words are used interchangeably, which is why 'UX research methodology' and 'UX research techniques' searches land on the same pages. Visual 1 sits here.

H3 'Is user research the same as UX research?' (PAA x2): Yes; first sentence starts 'Yes.' Hub: 'UX research, also called user research'. One sentence on market research vs user research to sharpen it (market research asks who buys and at what price; user research asks how people use and struggle).

H3 'How do UX research methods relate to academic research types?' (PAA cluster '7 types', 'four types', '7 types of qualitative'): see paaNote for the exact content and fact-check condition. Keep to 1 short paragraph + 1 short list; end with the UX meaning.

outline.h2: Which UX research method answers your research question?
outline.answerHint: The right UX research method is the one that answers your research question at the lowest cost: ask why users do something and you need interviews or observation, ask whether they can complete a task and you need usability testing, ask how many do it and you need analytics, a survey or an A/B test.
points: This is the owner's angle and the spine of the post. Answer the PAA 'most effective research techniques' in the first two sentences (no universal best; effective = fits the question and the product decision).

The router (Visual 2 + text version as a table): 8 question families, written as the question a PM actually asks, each -> primary method -> backup method -> what it cannot tell you. Families (our own wording; do not mirror formbricks rows): (1) 'What problem should we solve next?' -> user interviews / contextual inquiry; (2) 'How do people really do this work today?' -> contextual inquiry / field study / diary studies; (3) 'Where will people look for this?' (structure, labels) -> card sorting / tree testing; (4) 'Can people complete this task on our design?' -> usability testing (moderated) / unmoderated testing; (5) 'Which version performs better?' -> A/B testing (live product with enough traffic) / first-click test on a prototype; (6) 'How many users have this problem?' -> surveys / analytics; (7) 'Where do users drop off?' -> analytics and clickstream analytics, then interviews for the why; (8) 'Does this concept make sense before we build it?' -> concept testing / participatory design.

Rule of thumb under the table: a 'why' question needs a qualitative method, a 'how many' question a quantitative one, and 'what will you do in future' questions are unreliable in any method (people predict their own behavior poorly; state as practitioner reasoning, no statistic).

Card sorting appears here only as the method for family 3 (one sentence) with a link to /blog/card-sorting/ (anchor e.g. 'how open, closed and hybrid card sorting work'; CONDITIONAL on that post publishing today, else plain text).
Contextual inquiry: one sentence + link to /blog/contextual-inquiry/ (anchor e.g. 'contextual inquiry, where you watch users do real work').

outline.h2: What are the main types of UX research, and how do they differ?
outline.answerHint: The main types of UX research sort methods on two axes from Nielsen Norman Group's landscape: attitudinal methods capture what people say and behavioral methods capture what they do, while qualitative methods explain why and quantitative methods measure how many and how much.
points: First sentence must print 'types of UX research' (synonym) + 'research question' or 'product decision' in the next sentence.

Credit: Christian Rohrer, NN/g, 'When to Use Which User-Experience Research Methods' (2022, reviewed 2026). Explain the 3 dimensions in our words: attitudinal vs behavioral (carrier in keywordCarrierSecondary), qualitative vs quantitative (collected directly vs through an instrument; analysed by interpretation vs maths), context of use (natural, scripted, limited, none) with one method example each (field study; usability benchmarking; card sorting or concept testing; desirability study).

Visual 3: our own 2x2 map (behavioral <-> attitudinal on one axis, qualitative <-> quantitative on the other) placing about 12 methods; caption credits the NN/g framework; drawn new, NOT a copy of NN/g's chart (different layout, our method selection and placement checked against NN/g's text). Text version: a 4-quadrant list.

One short paragraph: methods that sit in the middle (usability testing can be qualitative with 5 users or quantitative with 40, NN/g; surveys can carry open questions). Name the future post 'quantitative UX research' in plain text as the place for the qual/quant deep dive (link-builder adds the link when it publishes).
Also mention moderated vs unmoderated and remote vs in-person as two practical axes (User Interviews field guide lists them; hub/usability-hub wording for moderated/unmoderated).

outline.h2: Which UX research methods fit each product stage?
outline.answerHint: UX research methods follow the product stage: generative methods such as interviews and field studies shape what to build, formative evaluative methods such as card sorting, tree testing and usability testing improve the design, and summative methods such as A/B testing, benchmarking and analytics measure the product after launch.
points: NN/g time dimension (strategize, design, launch and assess) mapped to generative, formative, summative; add 'continuous research' after launch (User Interviews: NPS and feedback surveys, product analytics, support feedback).
Print 'summative evaluation' once next to 'formative' (entity).

Visual 4: stage strip (left to right) with 3-4 methods per stage AND the matching step of our programme underneath (research framing; generative fieldwork 7-15 days; evaluative studies 4-8 days: 'Card sorts, tree tests and concept tests check the early information architecture and design concepts'). Quote hub step bodies; do not invent outputs for steps.
Keep generative vs evaluative to this section; name the future post 'generative vs evaluative research' in plain text (link later). Do not restate the hub FAQ wording; paraphrase it.

outline.h2: UX research methods compared, sample size, study length and output
outline.answerHint: UX research methods differ most in sample size, study length and main output: qualitative usability testing needs about 5 users per round, interviews 10-15 per user group, and quantitative studies about 40 participants or enough traffic for statistical significance, while outputs range from findings and quotes to metrics and an information architecture.
points: One sentence introduces the table (table-intro rule) and calls it 'a one-table UX research methods cheat sheet'. Visual 5 = this table as a spec-card infographic; text version = the markdown table.

Columns: method | answers | data type | data source | sample size | study length | main output | moderation. Rows (12): user interviews (hub 10-15 per user group, one hour each); contextual inquiry (hub 4-6 users, on-site in our programme, about 2 hours a session per the contextual-inquiry post); field study; diary studies (days to weeks; NN/g glossary 'days or months'); surveys (large samples; no fixed number, depends on the margin of error you need); focus group (NN/g glossary 6-9 people; NN/g landscape says 3-12; print one with its source, fact-checker picks); concept testing; card sorting (hub 30-50 in our programme, one row only); tree testing (hub 30-50 alongside the card sort); usability testing (5 per qualitative round, 40 quantitative, NN/g; 1-3 weeks per round, usability hub); A/B testing (enough traffic for statistical significance; live product); analytics and clickstream analytics (existing data; no recruiting).

Under the table, 3 short family paragraphs (talk to users / watch users / measure users) that mention first-click test, five-second test, eyetracking (needs special equipment; behavioral), participatory design, usability benchmarking and heuristic evaluation (expert review, no users; progress.com), each with one fact.
Print 'user research techniques' once here (synonym).
ONE cross-hub link: /services/usability-testing-services/ (anchor 'usability testing services') in the usability testing row's paragraph.

Lead moment 1 (end of section): sample sizes for quantitative methods and recruiting hard-to-reach users are where in-house plans stall; one natural sentence that our programme schedules participant recruitment as its own step (hub: 3-6 days).

outline.h2: How do you combine UX research methods in one study?
outline.answerHint: You combine UX research methods by letting each one answer the question the previous one raised: analytics shows where users drop off, interviews explain why, a card sort or tree test fixes the structure, a usability test checks the fix, and an A/B test measures it on the live product.
points: Visual 6: combination chain (5 linked steps, what each hands to the next). Text version as an ol.
Explain triangulation in one sentence (two methods agreeing on a finding is stronger evidence than one).
Worked illustrative example (label it illustrative, no client): the triage intro's 'trial users stall at setup' question taken through 3 methods with what each produced. No outcome percentage.

Our programme as the real-world pattern: research plan -> recruitment -> generative fieldwork (interviews + contextual inquiry) -> evaluative studies (card sorts, tree tests, concept tests) -> synthesis (Dovetail tagging, 2-4 personas, 1 journey map per persona, JTBD opportunity map, 90-minute readout). Link journey maps to /blog/customer-journey-map-template/ (anchor e.g. 'customer journey map template').

Lead moment 2: synthesis across methods is where findings fragment; one sentence pointing to how our 5-step programme ends in one readout (deep link /services/ux-research-services/#how-does-the-ux-research-process-work, anchor e.g. 'how our five-step research programme runs').

outline.h2: Which UX research methods work on a small budget or a tight deadline?
outline.answerHint: On a small budget, the UX research methods that still answer a research question are 5-user usability tests, a handful of interviews with existing customers, unmoderated tree tests and the analytics you already have; what you give up is sample breadth, hard-to-recruit users and observation in the real setting.
points: Table or 2-column list: shortcut -> what it still tells you -> what you lose (e.g. recruit from your customer list instead of a panel -> fast, but biased to current users; unmoderated instead of moderated -> scale, but no follow-up questions; remote interviews instead of contextual inquiry -> cheaper, but recall instead of observation).
Hub fact: 'UX research for a startup, for example 8-10 user interviews, shows which problem to solve' (hub FAQ). Use it as the minimum viable study example.
Maze's 'buy-in, budget and time' point: do not quote it; make our own point that the cheapest useful study is the one whose answer changes a decision.

outline.h2: Which mistakes make UX research methods give the wrong answer?
outline.answerHint: UX research methods give the wrong answer when the method does not match the research question: asking users to predict what they will do, running a survey to learn why, reporting a percentage from 5 usability participants, or testing navigation labels in an interview.
points: 6 mistakes as a ul, each with the fix: (1) method-first planning (the team runs the method it knows; NN/g notes many teams rely on one or two); (2) asking about future behavior; (3) surveys for why questions; (4) percentages from qualitative samples (5 users find problems, they do not measure rates; quantitative needs about 40, NN/g); (5) IA questions in interviews instead of card sorting/tree testing; (6) no research question written down before recruiting (the hub's research plan deliverable fixes it).
Different visual style from the router: no image here (6-image cap).

outline.h2: When should a research team choose and run the UX research methods for you?
outline.answerHint: Bring in a research team when the product decision needs two or more UX research methods, hard-to-recruit participants or on-site observation, or when nobody on your team can spend 4-8 weeks recruiting, running sessions and synthesising the findings.
points: MOFU close: 3 short signals (several methods needed; regulated or hard-to-recruit users such as clinicians, hub cost example; no in-house researcher). Then the offer (leadAngle).

Price once with deep link: $25,000-$60,000, 4-8 weeks, set by user groups, participants, number of methods and recruitment difficulty (anchor e.g. 'what sets the price of a research programme' -> /services/ux-research-services/#how-much-does-ux-research-cost).
Second UP link to the hub root with a varied anchor (e.g. 'our UX research programme'); the exact 'UX research services' anchor is used once early.
Sideways: /blog/choose-ux-research-agency/ (anchor e.g. 'how to compare research agencies before you hire one').
Close with /contact/ (anchor e.g. 'send us your research question').

Plain-text list of future cluster posts is NOT a separate section: name them in context where they fit (quantitative UX research in H2 3, generative vs evaluative research in H2 4, user persona template in H2 6 personas, importance of UX research and UX ROI in this H2's first paragraph, healthcare UX research next to the clinicians example). No links until each publishes.

faqs.q: Is UX research being replaced by AI?
faqs.hint: No. AI tools speed up transcription, tagging and first-pass synthesis, but synthetic users (AI profiles that mimic a user group) give overly favorable, shallow answers and cannot replace research with real people; NN/g (Maria Rosala and Kate Moran, 21 Jun 2024) says use them for desk research and hypotheses only. Our stance (home.ts): AI accelerates production, the judgment comes from research.

faqs.q: What is the 5-user rule for usability testing?
faqs.hint: Jakob Nielsen's guidance (NN/g, 2000) that 5 users per round find most usability problems in a qualitative test, so several small rounds beat one big one. It does not apply to quantitative studies (about 40, NN/g) or to card sorting. Same figures as H2 5. Fact-checker confirms the '85%' figure before it is printed; if unsure, omit the percentage.

faqs.q: What are the three types of user testing?
faqs.hint: There is no single standard trio; teams usually mean moderated vs unmoderated, qualitative vs quantitative, or remote vs in-person usability testing. One sentence each, usability hub wording for moderated/unmoderated.

faqs.q: What are the five steps of UX research?
faqs.hint: In our programme: research framing, participant recruitment, generative fieldwork, evaluative studies, synthesis and readout (hub). Name the steps only, with the deep link /services/ux-research-services/#how-does-the-ux-research-process-work; no durations list here (hub owns the process).

faqs.q: How many UX research methods should one study use?
faqs.hint: Usually 2-3: one to find or explain the problem and one to check or measure the answer (NN/g: nearly every project benefits from more than one method). Our programme runs generative fieldwork and evaluative studies in one engagement (hub).
